1.pericope_label: Ephraim feedeth on wind, and followeth after the east wind: he daily increaseth lies and desolation; and they do make a covenant with the Assyrians, and oil is carried into Egypt
debates: What the east wind stands for
Why Judah is arraigned after being called faithful
Whether Jacob here names the patriarch or the kingdom
outliers: Ellicott alone glosses Jacob in this verse as the northern kingdom, where Keil and Delitzsch make the name the link to the patriarch himself and Wesley takes it to cover Ephraim and Judah together
Calvin explains his earlier praise of Judah as comparative only, belonging to the worship still kept at Jerusalem and not to their manners, so that the controversy here is no contradiction
themes: A man filling his mouth with air and calling it food
A wind that parches the tender growth
Lies twisted together in hope of making one truth
Oil sent south while a treaty is signed north

3.pericope_label: He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God
debates: Whether the heel-grasp shows merit or election
Who wept, the patriarch or the angel
Who the angel was
outliers: Calvin knows and rejects an explanation that gives the weeping to the angel, as one confessing defeat when he asked to be let go, and gives it instead to the patriarch as the humility of a man who did not come away whole
Calvin refuses to emend the closing words so that God speaks with him rather than with us, holding that the change is made only because interpreters can find no sense in the phrase as it stands
themes: A hand guided in the womb before there was any choice
A God who fights with the left hand and defends with the right
A man lame for life who would not let go
A traveller met by God before he knew it

5.pericope_label: Even the Lord God of hosts; the Lord is his memorial
debates: What the hosts are
Why the second table is named first
What turning to God requires
outliers: Ellicott corrects the connective, reading not therefore but a contrastive but do thou return, and finds an implied contrast between the patriarch and his degenerate descendants

Calvin grants that the order here, mercy and judgment before waiting upon God, is neither natural nor legitimate, and defends it on the ground that repentance is better tested by the second table than by worship
themes: A wrestler who condescended to be overpowered
Hosts standing on the right hand and the left of a throne
A touchstone laid against a hidden life
Hope made to carry the whole worship of God

7.pericope_label: He is a merchant, the balances of deceit are in his hand: he loveth to oppress
debates: Whether the word is a trade or a name
What the boast of prosperity proves
Whether the wealth was innocently got
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch set aside a reading that makes the fraud religious rather than commercial, an offering to God of false show for true reverence, on the ground that the prophet names weights and violence and not worship

Ellicott holds the English rendering obscures the fierceness of the line and would translate it as an address to Canaan with false balances in his hand, rather than a statement that Ephraim is a merchant
themes: A heavy weight to buy with and a light one to sell by
A trade turned into a mystery of iniquity
A man who loves the oppressing more than the gain
Books that no one can find a fault in

9.pericope_label: And I that am the Lord thy God from the land of Egypt will yet make thee to dwell in tabernacles, as in the days of the solemn feast
debates: Whether the verse is promise or threat
What the tabernacles are
What the days of the solemn feast name
outliers: Clarke says plainly that he does not think the feast of tabernacles is referred to at all and reads the whole verse as a threat of captivity, where Wesley takes the same words for blessings named in allusion to the joy of that very feast

Calvin sets aside three current readings and takes the verse for the announcement of a second redemption, since the first has lost its influence through their forgetfulness, so that God must eject them again in order to restore them again
themes: A people who forgot the day they were carried out
A tent pitched a second time so as to be remembered
Every good gift received straight from the hand that gives
Camps gathering out of the desert for sacrifice

10.pericope_label: I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets
debates: Whether the prophets meant are those of old or of the gospel
Whether the ruin of Gilead is past or still to come
What multiplied altars are worth
outliers: Gill refers the speaking by prophets not to the prophets of the Old Testament but to the apostles and teachers of the gospel, in whom the voice of Christ speaks, where the rest keep it to the prophets sent to Israel
Ellicott reads the ruin of Gilead and Gilgal as a past invasion attested by the conqueror’s own inscriptions, and notes that others take the same words as prophecy of a calamity still to come
themes: Every method tried and all of it in vain
A question asked with a laugh in it
Altars raised as thick as stone heaps in a field
A shrine deserted and never named again

12.pericope_label: And Jacob fled into the country of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept sheep
debates: Which flight is meant
Whether the two prophets are one man or two
What the retrospect is for
outliers: Clarke alone takes the second prophet of the verse for Joshua rather than Moses, and points out that the place where the covenant of circumcision was received on entering the land is the very Gilgal now made a seat of idolatry
Gill reports and rejects a reading that makes the flight the later one out of the field of Syria into Gilead, which would turn the verse into an aggravation of the idolatry of that place
themes: A fugitive with nothing but his hands
Fourteen years of keeping sheep for a wife
A people begotten a second time coming out of Egypt
One man stretching out his hand for a nation

14.pericope_label: Ephraim provoked him to anger most bitterly: therefore shall he leave his blood upon him, and his reproach shall his Lord return unto him
debates: What the bitterness is
Whose blood is left upon him
What his Lord means for a people who had renounced him
outliers: Calvin takes the word rendered bitterly for the high places of the false worship, so that the provoking was done in them, where the others read it of the bitterness of the provocation itself
Clarke reads the leaving of blood as guilt not removed, matching it with the saying that the wrath of God abides on the man who will not believe, so that the perdition is entirely of the man himself
themes: A name of pride taking the place of a name of grace
Sins bitter in themselves and bitter in what they bring
Blood left standing where it was shed
A Lord still owning a people who had disowned him
